root_draft.speaker: agent
root_draft.text: The Sleeping Ice makes a crossing, a salvage stop and a journey below the surface three ways of facing the same place: dirty white ice that preserves what it swallows and responds dangerously to warmth. The surface is sparse and still. A comfortable camp announces itself to blind shivven travelling inside the ice; their moving cracks and rumble let you follow the approach. Open ice beside the camp can develop an attackable breach, with a precisely warned first encounter and less certain later ones. Cold and constructed floors are real defences. Staying longer brings the larger story already designed for this biome: softened slabs give up preserved remains, apparently lifeless ground can spend its one movement, and insects and young wyrms foreshadow the apex below. Digging for what the ice kept and recovering someone taken beneath it are deliberate expeditions with readable danger and a way home. Frozen wrecks reward stopping; Lantern Deeps supplies its own persistent caves beneath qualifying ground. The choice is what to risk and recover before moving on, and what it takes to make a longer stay possible.

asks.title: ASK FIRST — What the journey has to mean
asks.picture: Your clan crosses a silent ice plateau, pauses at an abandoned expedition rig, and finds a way below. A longer stay needs warmth, and that warmth starts trouble around the camp.
asks.text: Which part of that journey makes your sentence true, and where does my proposed root give you the wrong picture?
asks.decision: F1/F2. “Nobody stays” could mean a place people usually traverse, or a place where a successful long stay still feels like an expedition. The existing settlement mechanics remain covered under either reading.
asks.why: F1/F2. “Nobody stays” could mean a place people usually traverse, or a place where a successful long stay still feels like an expedition. The existing settlement mechanics remain covered under either reading.
asks.guess: Crossing is the normal story; a salvage camp or buried refuge is an exceptional commitment that must earn its trouble. I recommend leading with the journey and showing what makes a stop costly.
asks.tree_change: If moving on is central, the root and walk follow arrival, a chosen stop and departure; the warm-base loop gets its own acceptance scene. If a hard-won refuge is equally central, routine occupation becomes part of the main walk too. If my linking idea is wrong, rewrite the root before deriving leaves. Existing mechanics and admitted backlog are not put up for removal; no reply means no approved root.

asks.title: A place forty people can occupy without forgetting where they are
asks.picture: A forty-person colony has made a warm, floored refuge. They still need to go outside for salvage. Compare a routine where the edge needs occasional attention with one where every workday is interrupted by another urgent crack.
asks.text: What should a normal day's compromise between comfort and danger look like once that refuge is working?
asks.decision: F2/F3. More heat already means more and larger breaches, and insulation/cold outside are already part of the design. The missing experience bar is how much useful work and quiet remain at colony scale. A fixed “three days” in the settings cannot answer that by itself.
asks.why: F2/F3. More heat already means more and larger breaches, and insulation/cold outside are already part of the design. The missing experience bar is how much useful work and quiet remain at colony scale. A fixed “three days” in the settings cannot answer that by itself.
asks.guess: A prepared refuge gets stretches of useful work; heating carelessly creates a visible trend toward trouble. I recommend making risk a reason to manage the camp, with enough quiet to notice the stillness.

asks.title: Enough warning to make a decision
asks.picture: The first crack appears while a worker is far from camp. Its letter gives an exact countdown. You can recall the worker, send someone to break the crack, or prepare to meet what comes through. The shipped first timer is 24 in-game hours; that is tuning, not a newly approved bar.
asks.text: Which preparations should that first countdown let a small travelling party finish, and what mistake should still cost them?
asks.decision: F2. The first breach being taught and timed is already settled. A countdown can still fail to give a traveller a useful response, or erase all danger by allowing every preparation.
asks.why: F2. The first breach being taught and timed is already settled. A countdown can still fail to give a traveller a useful response, or erase all danger by allowing every preparation.
asks.guess: Recall exposed people and make one deliberate response; ignoring the warning should leave them facing a real breach. I recommend that as the first scene's success and rejection pair.
asks.tree_change: A recall-and-response window needs dispersed workers, actual travel and an ordinary attack order before expiry. A fortification window also needs construction labour and material costs in the fixture. A deliberately narrow escape window needs an honest departure route and recovery of the party. Later warnings remain vague under every answer; this does not ask for a second teaching letter or precise later directions.

asks.title: Flooring a crack that has already started
asks.picture: A crack has opened outside. Before its timer ends, the crew completes a constructed floor across that spot. The rule that a burst cannot come through floor or hull is already fixed; the code currently checks open ice when placing the crack and does not check it again when releasing shivven.
asks.text: What should the crew see happen to that existing crack, and where should the pressure beneath it go?
asks.decision: F2/F3. The hull rule settles where a burst may emerge. It does not settle the story of a crack sealed after it began. This is a transition of a built capability, not an offer to remove breaches.
asks.why: F2/F3. The hull rule settles where a burst may emerge. It does not settle the story of a crack sealed after it began. This is a transition of a built capability, not an offer to remove breaches.
asks.guess: The floor visibly seals this opening; a warm camp can later attract another crack on eligible open ice. I recommend preserving both the successful local defence and the ongoing cost of warmth.
asks.tree_change: A sealed opening needs a completion-before-expiry control and no emergence through the new floor. Continued pressure beneath it needs an honest blocked state and a defined outcome when that floor is later lost. Movement to another opening needs a readable relocation, legal ice cells and the agreed warning treatment. No answer permits emergence through a floor, including in adjacent spawn cells.

asks.title: A decoy heater and a safer camp
asks.picture: A strong heater is enclosed behind flooring. A weaker working heater is exposed beside open ice. A shivven can reach the weaker one; the stronger one is either behind that barrier or beyond its sensing range. Today it selects the map's strongest working heater before considering its own range and route.
asks.text: What should that shivven do as it reaches the strongest warmth it can actually approach, and what should make a decoy succeed or fail?
asks.decision: F2/F3. Heat sensing and floor protection are settled. Lingering at a protected beacon, pursuing an exposed local source and ignoring everything because a remote heater won a global comparison produce very different player strategies.
asks.why: F2/F3. Heat sensing and floor protection are settled. Lingering at a protected beacon, pursuing an exposed local source and ignoring everything because a remote heater won a global comparison produce very different player strategies.
asks.guess: It follows warmth within reach and waits at a real barrier; a decoy can draw it somewhere useful only while it supplies a believable stronger local signal. A remote out-of-range heater should not make nearby heat cease to exist.
asks.tree_change: Strongest sensed source needs selection within the sensing boundary before pursuit. A stronger protected beacon that holds attention needs a visible waiting state and a source-off transition. Switching to accessible heat needs distinct targets and demonstrated target changes. Range and barrier cases remain separate: inability to travel is not inability to sense. No answer adds light, sound or vibration as a native sense.

asks.title: What makes a salvage stop worth the warmth
asks.picture: The party has reached a frozen hull and expedition rig. Spending the day recovering useful cargo means feeding and protecting a warm camp; passing by means arriving sooner. The ice-kept bodies and deliberate thaw/calving will add further finds when their existing backlog is built.
asks.text: What should the party bring away from a successful day's stop that makes you glad they took the risk?
asks.decision: F1/F2. The wreck field is built; the recovery story remains thin if its reward is indistinguishable from incidental scrap. This asks for the payoff, without re-pitching the passed learned technology, ship crust or rites.
asks.why: F1/F2. The wreck field is built; the recovery story remains thin if its reward is indistinguishable from incidental scrap. This asks for the payoff, without re-pitching the passed learned technology, ship crust or rites.
asks.guess: A useful haul of unusually well-preserved equipment or materials, with enough visible evidence of the failed expedition to make the stop memorable. I recommend a practical cargo payoff before adding another progression system.
asks.tree_change: A material payoff needs a complete salvage-and-haul scene with useful quantities and work costs. Recoverable equipment needs actual usable items and condition preserved. If the abandoned expedition's readable story is essential, add a bounded recognition requirement against a real scene; show a labelled mock before specifying its look. If the story is incidental, it stays advisory. Cold Ledger remains admitted campaign design, and its detailed props are not inferred from this answer.
